subject: Trump Backs Diesel Export Ban

Here's the latest in trending:New AI hit: Analysts weigh in on AI agent Muse, while Meta (META) tests human concierge for the app.Beyond obesity: Novo Nordisk (NVO) eyes the hair-loss market to boost direct-to-consumer sales.Fraud crackdown: Trump administration removes hundreds of thousands of Obamacare enrollees.

 Good morning! Here's the latest in trending: 

 New AI hit:  Analysts weigh in on AI agent Muse , while Meta ( META ) tests human concierge for the app.

 Beyond obesity: Novo Nordisk ( NVO ) eyes the hair-loss market to boost direct-to-consumer sales.

 Fraud crackdown:  Trump administration removes hundreds of thousands of Obamacare enrollees .

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Top News
 
 
 
 Economic impact 
 
 
 
Getty Images
 
 
President Trump has backed a ban on diesel exports, while Treasury Secretary Bessent said the U.S. is "examining whether it's feasible in terms of the overall refining capacity and whether a full or partial ban would work." But the big question is how it would impact prices in the long run as well as the broader economy.

 Zoom in:  Average diesel prices reached a record $6.53/gallon on Tuesday, up 77% Y/Y, data from the American Automobile Association showed. California and Washington had the highest average prices among states, at about $8.44/gal and $7.47/gal, respectively. While a diesel export ban would lower U.S. prices temporarily, experts warn that the follow-on effects would be more negative. "Of the 8M barrels of diesel traded globally by sea each day, the U.S. supplies about 1.5M of them – ~20%," the American Petroleum Institute noted. "Removing U.S. diesel from the market could result in reduced refinery runs, global economic damage and even higher U.S. prices." U.S. refiners could respond to an export ban by cutting output, which would put more upward pressure on diesel prices. "But cutting refinery runs would not reduce diesel production alone," the API said. "It would also mean producing less gasoline, jet fuel and other products at a time when global fuel supplies are already tight."

 Zoom out:  There are also knock-on effects for the broader economy. "With Mexico and other Latin American economies relying on U.S. diesel , a ban could boomerang back into U.S. grocery, agricultural and AI-related supply chains, hurting consumers," experts at the Atlantic Council have warned. Mexico is the top agricultural exporter to the U.S. and largely relies on diesel-powered truck transport to move the exports. And Mexico's diesel inventories are already low. "If Mexico lost access to U.S. diesel imports, physical outages could emerge in a matter of days, disrupting agricultural production," the Atlantic Council stated. "That would likely translate into higher grocery prices and tighter supply for food staples that Americans purchase."

 Bigger picture:  The U.S. has emerged as the supplier of last resort to the world during the Middle East war, with diesel exports surging to a weekly record of nearly 2M bbl/day last month, and a pause would send buyers across Europe and Latin America scrambling for alternatives. Europe, in particular, has been grappling with a severe fuel crisis and the U.S. political cycle may currently be the region's greatest risk factor , Seeking Alpha analyst Zoltan Ban warned. "With midterm elections coming up, the idea of implementing a diesel export ban is gaining traction among the political establishment," he observed. "The U.S. has been exporting about 500,000 b/d of diesel to Europe recently. If it were to lose those volumes, it would amount to a loss equivalent to about 1/7 of EU diesel demand."
